proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(u\in\mathcal R\).  By Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}additive\mbox{-}decomposition}\), the independence of \(U\) and \(G_\Gamma\), and the defining characteristic function of the centered Gaussian \(G_\Gamma\), for every \(t\in\mathbb R\) we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
\phi_X(tu)
&=\mathbb E\!\left[\exp\!\left\{it u^\top(U+G_\Gamma)\right\}\right]\\
&=\mathbb E\!\left[\exp\!\left\{it u^\top U\right\}\right]
  \mathbb E\!\left[\exp\!\left\{it u^\top G_\Gamma\right\}\right]\\
&=\phi_U(tu)\exp\!\left\{-\frac{t^2}{2}u^\top\Gamma u\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(|t|\geq 1\), Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}ray\mbox{-}lower\mbox{-}envelope}\) gives \(|\phi_U(tu)|>0\).  Thus the logarithms below are finite.  Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass{:}ray\mbox{-}lower\mbox{-}envelope}\) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}ray\mbox{-}upper\mbox{-}envelope}\) give, respectively,
\[
\log c-q_u\log(1+|t|)
\leq \log|\phi_U(tu)|
\leq \log C-q_u\log(1+|t|).
\]
Define the proof intermediate
\[
r_u(t):=-\frac{2}{t^2}\log|\phi_U(tu)|.
\]
Multiplication of the preceding inequalities by the negative number \(-2/t^2\) yields
\[
-\frac{2\log C}{t^2}
+\frac{2q_u\log(1+|t|)}{t^2}
\leq r_u(t)
\leq
-\frac{2\log c}{t^2}
+\frac{2q_u\log(1+|t|)}{t^2}.
\]
By the definition of the exponent map, \(0\leq q_u\leq Q<\infty\).  Since \(t^{-2}\to0\) and \(t^{-2}\log(1+|t|)\to0\) as \(|t|\to\infty\), both endpoints in this display converge to zero.  The squeeze theorem therefore gives
\[
r_u(t)\longrightarrow0.
\]
Taking moduli and logarithms in the characteristic-function factorization, which is legitimate because its two factors are nonzero for \(|t|\geq1\), now gives the exact identity
\[
-\frac{2}{t^2}\log|\phi_X(tu)|
=u^\top\Gamma u+r_u(t).
\]
Consequently,
\[
-\frac{2}{t^2}\log|\phi_X(tu)|
\longrightarrow u^\top\Gamma u
\qquad (|t|\to\infty).
\]

It remains to exhibit the recovery map.  The observed law \(P_X\) determines \(\phi_X(s)=\int_{\mathbb R^p}e^{is^\top x}\,dP_X(x)\).  For each \(u\in\mathcal R\), define the observable limit
\[
\ell_u(P_X):=\lim_{|t|\to\infty}
\left\{-\frac{2}{t^2}\log|\phi_X(tu)|\right\}.
\]
The preceding argument proves that this limit exists and equals \(u^\top\Gamma u\).  Hence coordinate rays give
\[
\Gamma_{ii}=\ell_{e_i}(P_X),
\]
and, for \(i<j\), pair-sum rays and polarization give
\[
\Gamma_{ij}=\Gamma_{ji}
=\frac{1}{2}\left\{
\ell_{e_i+e_j}(P_X)-\ell_{e_i}(P_X)-\ell_{e_j}(P_X)
\right\}.
\]
These displayed formulas are an explicit functional of \(P_X\) and recover every entry of the symmetric matrix \(\Gamma\).  In particular, any two admissible covariance matrices producing the same observed law under the stated ray envelopes have identical coordinate and pair-sum quadratic forms and therefore identical entries.  Finally, Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}greatest\mbox{-}divisor}\) specifies that this recovered \(\Gamma\), rather than an arbitrary covariance from another convolution representation, is the greatest Gaussian-divisor covariance that is the causal covariance target.  This proves both the asserted limit and identification from \(P_X\).

Fix a linear extension \(\pi\) of \(\preceq\), and let \(S=\operatorname{Pred}_{\pi}(T)\).  Positive definiteness of \(\Gamma\) gives the unique modified Cholesky factorization \(\Gamma=L_{\pi}D_{\pi}^{2}L_{\pi}^{\top}\), with positive diagonal \(D_{\pi}\).  For an auxiliary vector \(G_{\Gamma}=L_{\pi}D_{\pi}Z\), where the coordinates of \(Z\) are independent standard Gaussians, the residual of \((G_{\Gamma})_T\) after projection on its predecessors is \((D_{\pi})_{TT}Z_T\).  Hence
\[
 \frac{\gamma_{YT\cdot S}(\Gamma)}{\gamma_{TT\cdot S}(\Gamma)}
 =\frac{\operatorname{Cov}((G_{\Gamma})_Y,(D_{\pi})_{TT}Z_T)}
 {\operatorname{Var}((D_{\pi})_{TT}Z_T)}
 =\frac{(L_{\pi})_{YT}(D_{\pi})_{TT}^{2}}{(D_{\pi})_{TT}^{2}}
 =(L_{\pi})_{YT}.
\]
The denominator is positive because it is the Schur complement of the positive-definite principal block \(\Gamma_{SS}\).  If \(Y\in S\), both the conditional covariance and \((L_{\pi})_{YT}\) are zero, so the same identity holds at this boundary case.

This calculation relates, rather than equates by definition, the causal effect and the observable covariance functional.  Indeed, the assumptions on the sources give the structural equations
\[
 X=(I-L_{\pi}^{-1})X+L_{\pi}^{-1}A H+D_{\pi}Z.
\]
The coefficient matrix is acyclic in order \(\pi\), multiplication by the invertible \(L_{\pi}^{-1}\) preserves the full column rank of the source loading, and the source independence and nonconstancy assumptions are unchanged.  Under an intervention on \(T\), solving these equations shows that the derivative of the mean of coordinate \(Y\) with respect to the imposed value of \(T\) is \((L_{\pi})_{YT}\).  The greatest-divisor assumption makes the \(\Gamma\) used here the stipulated causal Gaussian covariance, while the source assumptions ensure that each such Cholesky mechanism is admissible.

It remains to characterize the possible sets \(S\).  Every predecessor set contains \(D=\{v:v\prec T\}\), contains no strict successor of \(T\), and has the form \(D\cup J\) with \(J\subseteq A\).  If \(w\in J\) and \(v\in A\) satisfies \(v\prec w\), then \(v\) also precedes \(T\) in \(\pi\), so \(v\in J\); thus \(J\) is an ideal.  Conversely, if \(J\in\mathcal J\), then both \(D\cup J\) and \(D\cup J\cup\{T\}\) are ideals of the full partial order.  A linear extension of \(D\cup J\), followed by \(T\), followed by a linear extension of the complement, therefore realizes \(D\cup J\) as exactly the predecessor set of \(T\).  Substitution in the displayed regression identity proves
\[
 \Theta_{TY}(\Gamma,\preceq)=\{\beta_J(\Gamma):J\in\mathcal J\}.
\]

For the singleton certificate, take an ideal edge \(J\to J\cup\{W\}\), put \(S=D\cup J\), and abbreviate
\[
 u=\gamma_{TT\cdot S},\quad v=\gamma_{WW\cdot S},\quad
 r=\gamma_{TW\cdot S},\quad d=\gamma_{YT\cdot S},\quad
 e=\gamma_{YW\cdot S}.
\]
Positive definiteness gives \(u>0\), \(v>0\), and \(uv-r^2>0\).  Schur complementation on \(W\) gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \beta_J-\beta_{J\cup\{W\}}
 &=\frac d u-\frac{d-re/v}{u-r^2/v}\\
 &=\frac{r(ue-dr)}{u(uv-r^2)}
 =\frac{r\{e-dr/u\}}{uv-r^2}\\
 &=\frac{\gamma_{TW\cdot S}\,
 \gamma_{YW\cdot(S\cup\{T\})}}{uv-r^2}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus equality across an ideal edge is equivalent to the product in the statement being zero.  The graph of ideals is connected: from any nonempty ideal one may delete a maximal element and remain an ideal, and repetition reaches the empty ideal.  Hence vanishing on every edge makes all \(\beta_J\) equal; conversely, a singleton fiber forces equality on every edge and hence forces every displayed product to vanish.  When \(W=Y\), the second factor is the positive conditional variance \(\gamma_{YY\cdot(S\cup\{T\})}\); when \(Y\in S\), both adjacent coefficients and the relevant conditional covariance are zero.  These cases use no extra overlap or margin assumption.

By \(\mathrm{prop:ideal\text{-}fiber}\), both fibers are indexed by the same finite family \(\mathcal J\).  Fix \(J\), put \(S=D\cup J\) and \(B=S\cup\{T\}\).  If \(Y\in B\), then \(Y\ne T\) and \(\beta_J(H)=\beta_J(H')=0\).  Otherwise block regression gives
\[
 \beta_J(H)=e_T^{\top}H_{BB}^{-1}H_{BY},\qquad
 \beta_J(H')=e_T^{\top}(H'_{BB})^{-1}H'_{BY}.
\]
Principal compression does not increase operator norm, the spectral lower bound gives \(\|H_{BB}^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}},\|(H'_{BB})^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\lambda^{-1}\), and the spectral upper bound gives \(\|H'_{BY}\|_2\le\Lambda\).  The inverse identity
\[
 H_{BB}^{-1}-(H'_{BB})^{-1}
 =H_{BB}^{-1}(H'_{BB}-H_{BB})(H'_{BB})^{-1}
\]
therefore yields, with \(\delta=\|H-H'\|_{\mathrm{op}}\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\beta_J(H)-\beta_J(H')|
 &\le \|H_{BB}^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|H_{BY}-H'_{BY}\|_2
 +\|H_{BB}^{-1}-(H'_{BB})^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|H'_{BY}\|_2\\
 &\le (\lambda^{-1}+\Lambda\lambda^{-2})\delta=L_\beta\delta.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Matching the point indexed by \(J\) in one finite set to the point with the same index in the other gives both directed Hausdorff bounds, hence
\[
 d_H(\Theta_{TY}(H,\preceq),\Theta_{TY}(H',\preceq))
 \le L_\beta\|H-H'\|_{\mathrm{op}}.
\]
No step divides by a difference between two branch effects, so the inequality remains valid when branches collide.

The fallback branch is deterministic and \(K_N\) then contains every matrix satisfying the spectral assumptions, so suppose the active-branch inequalities \(t_N\ge1\) and \(m_N\ge2\varepsilon_N\) hold.  For a real random variable \(R\in[-1,1]\), convexity of the exponential gives
\[
 e^{sR}\le\frac{1+R}{2}e^s+\frac{1-R}{2}e^{-s}.
\]
After taking expectations and centering, differentiating the logarithm of the right-hand side shows that its second derivative is the variance of a variable supported on \([-1,1]\), hence is at most one.  Integration from zero twice gives \(\mathbb E e^{s(R-\mathbb ER)}\le e^{s^2/2}\).  Exponential Markov optimization, applied to the real and imaginary parts of \(e^{it_Nu^\top X_k}\), consequently gives
\[
 P_X^N\!\left(\left|\widehat\phi_N(t_Nu)-\phi_X(t_Nu)\right|>\varepsilon_N\right)
 \le4\exp(-N\varepsilon_N^2/4)=\frac{\alpha_N}{|\mathcal R|}.
\]
The union bound therefore produces an event \(E_N\), uniformly in \(P_X\in\mathcal M\), such that \(P_X^N(E_N)\ge1-\alpha_N\) and the displayed error is at most \(\varepsilon_N\) for every \(u\in\mathcal R\).  This finite-ray concentration and the ensuing polarization specialize the characteristic-function architecture of \cite{BelomestnyTrabsTsybakov2019}; all constants needed here have been derived above.

Independence in the additive decomposition gives
\[
 |\phi_X(t_Nu)|=|\phi_U(t_Nu)|
 \exp\{-t_N^2u^\top\Gamma u/2\}.
\]
Because \(q_u\le Q\), \(u^\top\Gamma u\le\Lambda\|u\|_2^2\), and \(\|u\|_2^2\le2\) on \(\mathcal R\), the ray lower envelope implies \(|\phi_X(t_Nu)|\ge m_N\).  On \(E_N\), therefore, \(|\widehat\phi_N(t_Nu)|\ge m_N/2\), so the floor in the definition is inactive and both moduli lie in \([m_N/2,1]\).  The real logarithm has derivative at most \(2/m_N\) on that interval, whence
\[
 \left|\log|\widehat\phi_N(t_Nu)|-\log|\phi_X(t_Nu)|\right|
 \le2\varepsilon_N/m_N.
\]
Writing \(\ell_u=\log|\phi_U(t_Nu)|+q_u\log(1+t_N)\), the two envelope assumptions give \(\ell_u\in[\log c,\log C]\), while
\[
 \log|\phi_X(t_Nu)|+q_u\log(1+t_N)
 =-\frac{t_N^2}{2}u^\top\Gamma u+\ell_u.
\]
Centering \(\ell_u\) at \((\log c+\log C)/2\) and using the preceding logarithmic error proves, simultaneously,
\[
 |z_u-u^\top\Gamma u|
 \le t_N^{-2}\{\log(C/c)+4\varepsilon_N/m_N\}=w_N.
\]

Polarization now gives \(|(Z_N)_{ii}-\Gamma_{ii}|\le w_N\) and \(|(Z_N)_{ij}-\Gamma_{ij}|\le3w_N/2\).  Hence
\[
 \|Z_N-\Gamma\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le p\max_{i,j}|(Z_N-\Gamma)_{ij}|\le\Delta_N.
\]
If an eigenvalue of \(Z_N\) lies outside \([\lambda,\Lambda]\), its distance to that interval is at most \(\|Z_N-\Gamma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\), by the variational characterization of extreme eigenvalues and the spectral assumptions on \(\Gamma\).  Thus eigenvalue clipping obeys \(\|\widehat\Gamma_N-Z_N\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\Delta_N\), and the triangle inequality gives
\[
 \|\widehat\Gamma_N-\Gamma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\Delta_N.
\]
Consequently \(\Gamma\in K_N\) on \(E_N\).  The empirical characteristic function is continuous in the sample, modulus, maximum, and real logarithm are Borel on the floored domain, polarization is linear, and eigenvalue clipping is a continuous functional of a symmetric matrix.  The active and fallback branches are selected by deterministic inequalities.  Hence \(\widehat\Gamma_N\) and the compact-valued set \(K_N\) are measurable.  Combining the active and fallback cases proves every assertion.

First note that every coefficient in the fiber lies in the deterministic fallback interval.  Indeed, for \(B=D\cup J\cup\{T\}\) and \(Y\notin B\),
\[
 |\beta_J(H)|=|e_T^\top H_{BB}^{-1}H_{BY}|
 \le\lambda^{-1}\Lambda,
\]
whereas \(Y\in B\) gives \(\beta_J(H)=0\).  Thus the fallback \([ -\Lambda/\lambda,\Lambda/\lambda]\) covers the entire fiber with probability one.

On the active branch, let \(E_N\) be the simultaneous event supplied by \(\mathrm{thm:fourier\text{-}region}\).  It has probability at least \(1-\alpha_N\), and on it \(\|\widehat\Gamma_N-\Gamma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\Delta_N\).  The Lipschitz lemma gives, for every \(J\in\mathcal J\),
\[
 |\beta_J(\widehat\Gamma_N)-\beta_J(\Gamma)|\le2L_\beta\Delta_N.
\]
The ideal representation then places each true fiber point in its corresponding interval in \(C_N\).  Since \(\alpha_N\le\alpha\), this proves the uniform finite-sample coverage claim.

For the excess bound, take \(x\in C_N\) on \(E_N\).  For some \(J\), the point \(x\) lies in the clipped interval centered at \(\beta_J(\widehat\Gamma_N)\), and hence
\[
 \inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{TY}(\Gamma,\preceq)}|x-\theta|
 \le |x-\beta_J(\widehat\Gamma_N)|
 +|\beta_J(\widehat\Gamma_N)-\beta_J(\Gamma)|
 \le4L_\beta\Delta_N.
\]
Taking the supremum over \(x\) proves the claim.  All unions are finite.  Their endpoints are continuous functions of the clipped covariance matrix, and intersection with the fixed compact interval preserves nonemptiness because each center is already in that interval.  Thus \(C_N\) is a measurable nonempty compact random set.  The proof simultaneously covers all ideals and never selects an order or invokes a separation between coincident effects.

Let \(d=|\mathcal R|\), which is fixed because \(p\) is fixed.  On the active branch,
\[
 t_N^2=\frac{\log N}{4\Lambda},\qquad
 m_N=c(1+t_N)^{-Q}N^{-1/4},\qquad
 \varepsilon_N=2\sqrt{\frac{\log(4d/\alpha_N)}{N}}.
\]
Since \(\alpha_N=(N+1)^{-2}\) for all sufficiently large \(N\),
\[
 \frac{\varepsilon_N}{m_N}
 =O\!\left(N^{-1/4}(1+\sqrt{\log N})^Q\sqrt{\log N}\right)=o(1).
\]
It follows that the active-branch conditions eventually hold, uniformly over the model, and, because \(c<C\),
\[
 w_N=t_N^{-2}\{\log(C/c)+o(1)\}=O((\log N)^{-1}),qquad
 \Delta_N=O((\log N)^{-1}).
\]

Let \(E_N\) be the simultaneous Fourier event.  On \(E_N\), the Fourier-region theorem gives \(\|\widehat\Gamma_N-\Gamma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\Delta_N\); on its complement both matrices have spectra in \([\lambda,\Lambda]\), so their operator-norm distance is at most \(2\Lambda\).  Moreover \(P_X^N(E_N^c)\le\alpha_N\le(N+1)^{-2}\), uniformly in \(P_X\).  Therefore
\[
 \sup_{P_X\in\mathcal M}\mathbb E\|\widehat\Gamma_N-\Gamma\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le2\Delta_N+2\Lambda\alpha_N=O((\log N)^{-1}).
\]
The deterministic fiber Lipschitz inequality, applicable on every sample outcome, immediately yields
\[
 \sup_{P_X\in\mathcal M}\mathbb E,d_H(\Theta_{TY}(\widehat\Gamma_N,\preceq),
 \Theta_{TY}(\Gamma,\preceq))=O((\log N)^{-1}).
\]

Finally, on \(E_N\) the whole-fiber theorem gives inclusion of the true fiber and excess at most \(4L_\beta\Delta_N\), so the Hausdorff distance has the same bound.  On \(E_N^c\), both nonempty compact sets lie in \([ -\Lambda/\lambda,\Lambda/\lambda]\), and hence their Hausdorff distance is at most \(2\Lambda/\lambda\).  Consequently
\[
 \sup_{P_X\in\mathcal M}\mathbb E,d_H(C_N,\Theta_{TY}(\Gamma,\preceq))
 \le4L_\beta\Delta_N+(2\Lambda/\lambda)\alpha_N
 =O((\log N)^{-1}).
\]
All constants depend only on the fixed declared class constants, so each bound is uniform over \(\mathcal M\).

Let the affirmative construction be the theorem replacing \(\mathrm{oeq:smooth\text{-}splice}\), and write \(s_N=1/(600\log N)\).  Its two laws lie in \(\mathcal M_\star\), their product total variation tends to zero, and
\[
 \|\Gamma(s_N)-\Gamma(0)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 =s_N\|aa^\top\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\frac{54}{25}s_N.
\]
For any estimator \(\widetilde\Gamma_N\), let \(A_N\) be the event that its distance from \(\Gamma(0)\) is less than half this separation.  The triangle inequality implies that its loss under \(P_{1,N}\) is at least half the separation on \(A_N\), while its loss under \(P_{0,N}\) is at least half the separation on \(A_N^c\).  Consequently
\[
 \max_{j=0,1}\mathbb E_{P_{j,N}^{\otimes N}}
 \|\widetilde\Gamma_N-\Gamma(P_{j,N})\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \ge\frac{27}{50}s_N
 \{1-\|P_{0,N}^{\otimes N}-P_{1,N}^{\otimes N}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\}.
\]
This is a constant multiple of \((\log N)^{-1}\).  The estimator \(\widehat\Gamma_N\) from the expected-rate theorem is a single measurable, data-driven estimator and gives the matching upper bound uniformly on the containing class \(\mathcal M\), hence also on \(\mathcal M_\star\).

The two effect fibers are singletons.  Their Hausdorff separation is
\[
 |b(s_N)-b(0)|=\frac{(2/5)s_N}{1+s_N}\ge\frac{s_N}{5}.
\]
Applying the same event argument in the metric space \(\mathcal K(\mathbb R)\) gives a constant multiple of \((\log N)^{-1}\) as a lower bound for every measurable fiber estimator.  The plug-in fiber \(\Theta_{TY}(\widehat\Gamma_N,\preceq)\), together with the expected-rate theorem, gives the matching upper bound.  This proves both minimax equivalences without using an oracle nuisance.

For the confidence-set assertion, uniform honesty supplies a deterministic \(r_N\downarrow0\) such that, for all sufficiently large \(N\),
\[
 \inf_{P\in\mathcal M_\star}P^{\otimes N}
 \{\Theta_{TY}(\Gamma(P),\preceq)\subseteq S_N\}
 \ge1-\alpha-r_N.
\]
Thus \(P_{0,N}^{\otimes N}\{b(0)\in S_N\}\ge1-\alpha-r_N\), while honesty at \(P_{1,N}\), transferred to \(P_{0,N}\) by total variation, gives
\[
 P_{0,N}^{\otimes N}\{b(s_N)\in S_N\}
 \ge1-\alpha-r_N-|P_{0,N}^{\otimes N}-P_{1,N}^{\otimes N}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}.
\]
A union bound shows that both points belong to \(S_N\) with limiting lower probability at least \(1-2\alpha\).  On that event its diameter is at least \(|b(s_N)-b(0)|\), proving the final assertion.  No swap margin is used because both experiments lie on the exact singleton-collision stratum.

Let \(K=[-\sqrt{V_8},\sqrt{V_8}]^{d_4}\).  Centered covariances and fourth cumulants are polynomials in the raw moments of total degree at most four.  Their gradients are continuous and therefore bounded on the compact cube \(K\); the mean-value formula makes the combined moment-to-covariance-and-cumulant map Lipschitz on \(K\).

The scalar maximum map \(x\mapsto\max\{x,(3/2)a_{\min}^4\}\) is one-Lipschitz.  Its range is bounded below by the positive number \((3/2)a_{\min}^4\).  Hence the functions
\[
 x\longmapsto (x/3)^{1/4},\qquad x\longmapsto3^{-1}(x/3)^{-3/4}
\]
have bounded derivatives on the relevant compact range.  The reconstructed loading coordinates, and then the polynomial map \((\Sigma,a)\mapsto\Sigma-aa^\top\), are consequently Lipschitz on the image of \(K\).  Finally, eigenvalue clipping to \([\lambda,\Lambda]\) is the metric projection, in Frobenius norm, onto the closed convex set \(\{H:\lambda I\preceq H\preceq\Lambda I\}\), and metric projection onto a closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional Hilbert space is nonexpansive: expanding the two projection variational inequalities and adding them proves this directly.  Since operator norm is bounded by Frobenius norm, the complete map \(F_{p,M_8,a_{\min}}\) is globally Lipschitz from Euclidean norm on \(K\) to operator norm.  Therefore the quotient defining \(C_{\mathrm{Lap}}\) is bounded, and \(C_{\mathrm{Lap}}<\infty\).  The argument explicitly includes both the maximum-floor kink and all eigenvalue-clipping kinks.

Let \(\mu\) denote the vector of true raw moments of total degree one through four and let \(\widehat\mu\) be its coordinatewise clipped empirical version.  If a monomial has total degree \(r\le4\), then its square is bounded by \(1+\|X\|^8\).  Thus every coordinate has variance at most \(V_8\), and the iid assumption gives
\[
 \mathbb E\|\widehat\mu-\mu\|_2^2\le\frac{d_4V_8}{N}.
\]
The true moment coordinates lie in the clipping interval by Cauchy--Schwarz, so clipping cannot increase their Euclidean error.  Jensen's inequality and Markov's inequality consequently give
\[
 \mathbb E\|\widehat\mu-\mu\|_2\le\sqrt{\frac{d_4V_8}{N}},
 \qquad
 P^{\otimes N}\{\|\widehat\mu-\mu\|_2>r_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}\}\le\alpha.
\]

For the standardized Laplace variable, \(\mathbb EH_{\mathrm{Lap}}^4=6\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(H_{\mathrm{Lap}})=1\), so its fourth cumulant is three.  Multilinearity of cumulants, independence of \(U\) and the Gaussian component, and vanishing fourth Gaussian cumulants yield
\[
 \kappa_{TTTT}(X)=3(a_T^{\mathrm{Lap}})^4,qquad
 \kappa_{iTTT}(X)=3a_i^{\mathrm{Lap}}(a_T^{\mathrm{Lap}})^3.
\]
At the true moment vector the cumulant floor is inactive because \(|a_T^{\mathrm{Lap}}|\ge a_{\min}\).  The reconstruction returns \(\widetilde a=\operatorname{sgn}(a_T^{\mathrm{Lap}})a^{\mathrm{Lap}}\), so \(\widetilde a\widetilde a^\top=a^{\mathrm{Lap}}(a^{\mathrm{Lap}})^\top\).  Since
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(X)=a^{\mathrm{Lap}}(a^{\mathrm{Lap}})^\top+\Gamma(P),
\]
and the true \(\Gamma(P)\) already has spectrum in \([\lambda,\Lambda]\), it follows that \(F_{p,M_8,a_{\min}}(\mu)=\Gamma(P)\).  The global Lipschitz lemma now gives, on every sample outcome,
\[
 \|\widehat\Gamma_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}-\Gamma(P)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le C_{\mathrm{Lap}}\|\widehat\mu-\mu\|_2.
\]
Taking expectations proves the uniform \(O(N^{-1/2})\) covariance claim.  Applying the deterministic fiber Lipschitz lemma proves the uniform \(O(N^{-1/2})\) Hausdorff claim.

On the event \(\|\widehat\mu-\mu\|_2\le r_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}\), the same two inequalities give, simultaneously for every \(J\in\mathcal J\),
\[
 |\beta_J(\widehat\Gamma_N^{\mathrm{Lap}})-\beta_J(\Gamma(P))|
 \le L_\beta C_{\mathrm{Lap}}r_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}.
\]
The exact ideal-fiber representation therefore places every true compatible effect in its corresponding interval in \(C_N^{\mathrm{Lap}}\).  The preceding probability bound proves coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) for every \(N\), uniformly over \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{Lap}}\).  All maps used are Borel: coordinate clipping, polynomial moment maps, the positive floor, reciprocal powers above that floor, spectral clipping, and a finite union of compact intervals.  Positivity of the cumulant denominator is supplied exactly by the stated treatment-loading condition.

theorem.statement:
For every sufficiently large \(N\), there are Borel laws \(P_{0,N},P_{1,N}\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{col}}\subseteq\mathcal M_\star\) and \(s_N=1/(600\log N)\) such that \(\Gamma(P_{0,N})=\Gamma(0)\), \(\Gamma(P_{1,N})=\Gamma(s_N)\), and \(\|P_{0,N}^{\otimes N}-P_{1,N}^{\otimes N}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\to0\).  Both laws have a one-dimensional, unit-variance, Gaussian-indecomposable source representation with \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=1\) and \(\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}<A_{\max}=3\), obey \(q_u=2\) on every \(u\in\mathcal R\) with common lower envelope constant \(2/5\) and upper envelope constant \(60\), satisfy \(\mathbb E\|X\|^8\le M_8=50000000\), and have the displayed covariance as their greatest Gaussian-divisor covariance.  Moreover,
\[
 \Theta_{TY}(\Gamma(P_{0,N}),\preceq)=\{b(0)\},\qquad
 \Theta_{TY}(\Gamma(P_{1,N}),\preceq)=\{b(s_N)\}.
\]
theorem.proof_tex:
We give the construction and verify each class condition.  Fix \(m=6\), \(\eta=1/10\), \(\kappa=1/20\), and let
\[
 f_0(x)=(1-\eta)\frac{e^{-\sqrt2|x|}}{\sqrt2}+\eta c_6(1+x^2)^{-6},
 \qquad c_6=\frac{256}{63\pi}.
\]
Its characteristic function is the positive even function
\[
 \phi_0(t)=\frac{1-\eta}{1+t^2/2}+\eta e^{-|t|}
 \left(1+|t|+\frac{4|t|^2}{9}+\frac{|t|^3}{9}
 +\frac{|t|^4}{63}+\frac{|t|^5}{945}\right).
\]
The second term follows by inserting the gamma integral for \((1+x^2)^{-6}\), interchanging two nonnegative integrals, and evaluating the resulting Gaussian Fourier integral.  In particular, \(\phi_0(t)>0\).

Choose a fixed even \(C^\infty\) function \(\chi\), valued in \([0,1]\), equal to one on \([-1,1]\) and zero off \([-2,2]\).  For \(M\ge1\), put \(\delta=\kappa M^{-2}\) and
\[
 \phi_{1,M}(t)=\phi_0(t)\left[1+\chi(t/M)\{e^{-\delta t^2/2}-1\}\right].
\]
We first prove that this is a characteristic function for every sufficiently large \(M\).  With the Fourier convention \(\widehat f(t)=\int e^{itx}f(x)\,dx\), write
\[
 f_{1,M}=f_0*\varphi_\delta+h_M,qquad
 \widehat h_M(t)=\phi_0(t)\{1-\chi(t/M)\}\{1-e^{-\kappa(t/M)^2/2}\},
\]
where \(\varphi_\delta\) is the centered Gaussian density of variance \(\delta\).  Define
\[
 b_M(z)=M^2\phi_0(Mz)\{1-\chi(z)\}\{1-e^{-\kappa z^2/2}\}.
\]
For each \(0\le j\le12\), there is a finite constant \(B_j\), independent of \(M\), such that \(\|b_M^{(j)}\|_1\le B_j\).  To see this rather than assume it, note first that the factor \(1-\chi\) vanishes on \(|z|\le1\).  On \(|z|\ge1\), direct differentiation of
\[
 \frac{M^2}{1+M^2z^2/2}=\frac{2}{z^2+2M^{-2}}
\]
is bounded in derivative order \(j\) by \(C_j|z|^{-2-j}\).  Each differentiated Student summand is bounded by a finite sum of terms
\[
 M^{2+j+r}|z|^r e^{-M|z|}
 =|z|^{-2-j}(M|z|)^{2+j+r}e^{-M|z|},\qquad 0\le r\le5,
\]
whose last factor is uniformly bounded for \(M|z|\ge1\).  Derivatives of \(\chi\) are supported on \(1\le|z|\le2\), and derivatives of \(1-e^{-\kappa z^2/2}\) are bounded.  The product rule and integrability of \(|z|^{-2-j}\) establish the asserted \(B_j\).

Fourier inversion, followed by twelve integrations by parts, now gives a constant \(A_{12}<\infty\), independent of \(M\), for which
\[
 |h_M(x)|\le A_{12}M^{-1}(1+M|x|)^{-12}.
\]
Indeed, changing variables \(t=Mz\) gives \(h_M(x)=(2\pi M)^{-1}\int e^{-iMxz}b_M(z)\,dz\); the bounds using \(B_0\) and \(B_{12}\) control respectively small and large \(M|x|\).  On the other hand, for \(\delta\le1\), restriction of the Gaussian convolution to \(|z|\le1\) gives
\[
 (f_0*\varphi_\delta)(x)
 \ge a_6(1+x^2)^{-6},\qquad a_6=\eta c_6 3^{-7}>0,
\]
because \(1+(x-z)^2\le3(1+x^2)\) and \(P\{|N(0,\delta)|\le1\}\ge1/3\).  Since \((1+x^2)^6\le(1+M|x|)^{12}\),
\[
 \frac{|h_M(x)|}{(f_0*\varphi_\delta)(x)}\le\frac{A_{12}}{a_6M}.
\]
Thus \(f_{1,M}\ge0\) once \(M\ge2A_{12}/a_6\).  Also \(\widehat h_M(0)=0\), so \(f_{1,M}\) integrates to one.  It is even, and hence centered.  This proves global density positivity and Borel measurability; it does not treat the splice multiplier itself as a characteristic function.  This Fourier-tail domination is the smooth finite-moment implementation of the compensation architecture in \cite{Meister2006}.

Because \(\widehat h_M\) vanishes on a neighborhood of zero and the displayed spatial bound makes \(|x|^8h_M(x)\) integrable, differentiation under the Fourier integral gives \(\int x^jh_M(x)\,dx=0\) for \(0\le j\le8\).  The beta integral gives, for the Student component \(S_6\),
\[
 \mathbb E S_6^{2j}=\frac{\Gamma(j+1/2)\Gamma(11/2-j)}{\sqrt\pi\Gamma(11/2)},\qquad 0\le j\le5.
\]
Combining this with the standardized-Laplace moments \((2j)!/2^j\) yields
\[
 \mu_2=\frac{41}{45},\quad \mu_4=\frac{227}{42},\quad
 \mu_6=\frac{17011}{210},\quad \mu_8=\frac{204121}{90}.
\]
Consequently, if \(H_{1,M}\) has density \(f_{1,M}\), its first eight moments equal those of \(H_0+N(0,\delta)\), where \(H_0\) has density \(f_0\), and
\[
 \mathbb E H_{1,M}^8
 =\mu_8+28\delta\mu_6+210\delta^2\mu_4
 +420\delta^3\mu_2+105\delta^4
 \le\frac{554293}{90}
\]
for \(0\le\delta\le1\).  Thus the required moment bound is uniform in \(M\).

The multiplier in \(\phi_{1,M}\) lies between \(e^{-2\kappa}\) and one, equals \(e^{-\delta t^2/2}\) for \(|t|\le M\), and equals one for \(|t|\ge2M\).  Both \(\phi_0\) and \(\phi_{1,M}\) therefore have a positive constant times \(|t|^{-2}\) as their tail.  If either source admitted a Gaussian divisor of variance \(r>0\), the residual characteristic function would have modulus \(e^{rt^2/2}|\phi(t)|\), which diverges and contradicts the universal modulus bound one for characteristic functions.  Both sources are consequently Gaussian-indecomposable.

We next establish indistinguishability.  Fix \(v=1/10\) and define scalar observed densities
\[
 q_{0,M}=f_0*\varphi_{v+\delta},\qquad q_{1,M}=f_{1,M}*\varphi_v.
\]
Their Fourier difference is
\[
 \widehat D_M(t)=e^{-vt^2/2}\phi_0(t)\{1-\chi(t/M)\}
 \{1-e^{-\delta t^2/2}\},
\]
which vanishes on \([-M,M]\).  The Student component and restriction of the convolution to a fixed Gaussian interval give a constant \(a_v>0\), uniformly for \(0\le\delta\le\kappa\), such that
\[
 q_{0,M}(x)\ge a_v(1+x^2)^{-6}.
\]
For \(0\le j\le6\), the product rule, the rational derivative bounds already proved, and the formula for derivatives of the Gaussian factor yield
\[
 |\widehat D_M^{(j)}(t)|
 \le C_j(1+|t|)^{2j+2}e^{-vt^2/2}\mathbf 1\{|t|\ge M\}.
\]
The factors produced by differentiating \(\chi(t/M)\) are at most one for \(M\ge1\), and those produced by \(1-e^{-\kappa t^2/(2M^2)}\) are covered by the displayed polynomial.  The derivative envelope permits differentiation under Fourier inversion and gives \(\widehat{x^jD_M}=i^{-j}\widehat D_M^{(j)}\) for \(0\le j\le6\).  Applying \(\mathrm{lem:parseval\text{-}identity}\) to each \(x^jD_M\) and expanding \((1+x^2)^6\) gives
\[
 \int(1+x^2)^6|D_M(x)|^2\,dx
 =\frac1{2\pi}\sum_{j=0}^6\binom6j\|\widehat D_M^{(j)}\|_2^2.
\]
The Gaussian tail integral, integrated once after extracting its polynomial factor, is bounded by \(C(1+M)^{29}e^{-vM^2}\).  It follows that
\[
 \chi^2(q_{1,M},q_{0,M})
 =\int\frac{|D_M(x)|^2}{q_{0,M}(x)}\,dx
 \le A(1+M)^{29}e^{-vM^2}
\]
for a fixed \(A<\infty\).  Independence and Fubini give
\[
 1+\chi^2(q_{1,M}^{\otimes N},q_{0,M}^{\otimes N})
 =\{1+\chi^2(q_{1,M},q_{0,M})\}^N.
\]
Taking \(M^2=30\log N\) makes \(vM^2=3\log N\), and therefore the product chi-square divergence tends to zero.  Cauchy--Schwarz applied to the likelihood-ratio difference gives total variation at most one half the square root of this divergence, so the product total variation tends to zero.

It remains to embed these scalar experiments in the declared causal class.  Let \(a=(1,2/5,1)^\top\), let \(\Gamma_\star\) be the displayed matrix, and put \(\overline\Gamma=\Gamma_\star-vaa^\top\).  Its leading principal minors are \(9/10\), \(189/250\), and \(294/625\), so it is positive definite.  Apply to both scalar experiments the same Markov kernel \(z\mapsto az+G_{\overline\Gamma}\).  Conditional Jensen applied to the likelihood ratio proves that chi-square divergence cannot increase under this kernel.  Define
\[
 P_{0,N}=\mathcal L(aH_{1,M}+G_{\Gamma_\star}),\qquad
 P_{1,N}=\mathcal L(aH_0+G_{\Gamma_\star+\delta aa^\top}).
\]
These are precisely the two kernel images in the opposite scalar labeling, so their product total variation tends to zero.  Set \(s_N=\delta=1/(600\log N)\).

We verify the fixed numerical class.  The leading principal minors of \(\Gamma_\star-I/10\) are \(9/10\), \(13/20\), and \(8109/25000\); those of \(4I-\Gamma(1)\) are \(2\), \(126/25\), and \(44/125\).  Since \(\Gamma(s)\) increases in Loewner order, \(I/10\prec\Gamma(s)\prec4I\) for \(0\le s\le1\).  On every coordinate or pair-sum ray, \(|a^\top u|\in\{2/5,1,7/5,2\}\).  For \(t\ge1\),
\[
 \frac12\le\frac{(1+t)^2}{1+(a^\top u)^2t^2/2}\le\frac{27}{2}.
\]
The lower envelope is thus at least \((9/20)e^{-1/10}>2/5\).  If \(P_5\) denotes the polynomial in the displayed Student characteristic function, direct expansion gives
\[
 \sum_k [z^k]\{(1+z)^2P_5(z)\}\,k!=\frac{4714}{63}.
\]
Using \(e^{-z}z^k\le k!\) and \((1+t)^2\le(25/4)(1+|a^\top u|t)^2\) yields the common upper constant
\[
 \frac9{10}\frac{27}{2}+\frac1{10}\frac{25}{4}\frac{4714}{63}
 =\frac{37117}{630}<60.
\]
The splice multiplier can only decrease the modulus, so both sources obey the common exponent-two envelopes.

Moreover, \(\|a\|_2^2=54/25\), and the eighth-power triangle inequality and the Gaussian coupling \(G_\Gamma=\Gamma^{1/2}Z_3\) give
\[
 \mathbb E\|aH+G_\Gamma\|^8
 \le2^7\left\{(54/25)^4(554293/90)+4^4(3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot9)\right\}
 <50000000.
\]
After rescaling each scalar source to unit variance and multiplying its loading by the corresponding standard deviation, the law of \(U\) is unchanged.  The loading remains rank one and its squared norm is at most \((54/25)(86/45)=516/125<9\).  The source sign and column-order conventions hold because all entries of \(a\) are positive.

For every direction \(u\), the source characteristic function is either \(\phi_H(t a^\top u)\), which has a polynomial tail, or is identically one.  Hence
\[
 -2t^{-2}\log|\phi_X(tu)|\longrightarrow u^\top\Gamma u.
\]
If \(\Delta\) were any Gaussian-divisor covariance, the modulus bound on the residual characteristic function would imply \(u^\top\Delta u\le u^\top\Gamma u\) for every \(u\), hence \(\Delta\preceq\Gamma\).  Since the displayed \(\Gamma\) is itself a divisor, it is the greatest divisor.

Finally, direct substitution along \(\Gamma(s)=\Gamma_\star+saa^\top\) gives
\[
 \Gamma_{WY}(s)-\frac{\Gamma_{WT}(s)\Gamma_{TY}(s)}{\Gamma_{TT}(s)}=0,
 \qquad
 \frac{\Gamma_{TY}(s)}{\Gamma_{TT}(s)}=\frac{3/5+s}{1+s}=b(s).
\]
Under the partial order whose only relation is \(T\prec Y\), the only treatment-predecessor ideals are \(\varnothing\) and \(\{W\}\); the ideal-fiber proposition therefore gives \(\Theta_{TY}(\Gamma(s),\preceq)=\{b(s)\}\).  Thus both constructed laws belong to \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{col}}\) and satisfy every assertion.

added_lemmas.statement: Under the Fourier convention \(\widehat g(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{itx}g(x)\,dx\) on \(L^1(\mathbb R)\cap L^2(\mathbb R)\), extended continuously to \(L^2(\mathbb R)\), every square-integrable \(g\) satisfies \(\|g\|_2^2=(2\pi)^{-1}\|\widehat g\|_2^2\).

proposed_statement_changes.proposed: For every \(N\), \(\inf_{P_X\in\mathcal M}P_X^N\{\Theta_{TY}(\Gamma,\preceq)\subseteq C_N\}\ge1-\alpha\). On the simultaneous covariance event, \(\operatorname{ex}(C_N,\Theta_{TY}(\Gamma,\preceq))\le4L_\beta\Delta_N\).
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The finite-sample coverage and excess claims follow from the frozen assumptions. The appended blanket nonnestedness assertion does not: the parameterized Fourier class can be empty or can exclude the proposed witnesses for restrictive fixed loading, moment, envelope, or exponent constants, and no assumptions characterize membership in the nonlinear additive-error comparator. Removing that ancillary assertion is an honest narrowing rather than treating an unproved generic-class certificate as established.

proposed.statement: For every \(N\), \(\inf_{P_X\in\mathcal M}P_X^N\{\Theta_{TY}(\Gamma,\preceq)\subseteq C_N\}\ge1-\alpha\). On the simultaneous covariance event, \(\operatorname{ex}(C_N,\Theta_{TY}(\Gamma,\preceq))\le4L_\beta\Delta_N\).
proposed.justification: The theorem supplies finite-sample simultaneous coverage of the complete mixed-noise effect fiber, rather than asymptotic coverage of one effect after order-confidence and adjustment-set steps.
proposed.gap: Wang--Kolar--Drton's Algorithm 3 and Lemma 1 work in a causally sufficient recursive additive-error model with mutually independent centered coordinate errors and order identifiability from nonlinear functions or linear non-Gaussian errors; their effect interval is asymptotically valid for one total effect conditional on order-set and adjustment-interval validity. The present nonnested model permits latent common sources, identifies a greatest Gaussian divisor by Fourier tails, and gives finite-sample simultaneous inclusion of every partial-order-compatible Cholesky effect.
proposed.consumer: The \(\texttt{pcalg::ida}\) workflow can report a confidence-enlarged set of all compatible effects rather than a selected list.
